headline_en: Long quiet stretch, then maximum in 10 seconds
note_en: It plays loud for the shortest time of the three. After the first chord it stays quiet for a long while, starts to swell near the back, and reaches its maximum within 10 seconds.

headline_en: Holds the loud sound the longest
note_en: It rises straight to its loudest and holds loud playing longer than either of the other two. The middle drops by just one notch.
It reaches its loudest within 9 seconds, then sinks the middle deeper than Hamelin does. From there it builds up again.
At 2:52 it is shorter than the other two. It starts out loud, and it begins to swell earlier than Litton and Tilson Thomas do.
At 3:31 it runs 39 seconds longer than Ozawa. It sinks the quiet passage at the start deep, then builds up in two stages.
At 2:01 it is 35 seconds shorter than Noseda. It moves through the quiet passage quickly and climbs to its loudest in just a few seconds at the end.
It reaches its loudest at the last tutti, when the whole orchestra gathers again. It also ends the loudest of the three.
It keeps the big early passages one notch lower and saves the loudest sound for near the end. It doesn't linger on loud playing either.

headline_en: Near maximum from the first note
note_en: At 2:09 it is the shortest of the three. It enters near maximum from the very first note and sings at its loudest early on.
It builds toward the final tutti 11 seconds earlier than Previn. After the climax it sets the ending down alone, quietly.
The gap between quiet and loud is wider than in the other two. It sinks to its softest just before the end, then jumps to loud in one move.
It rings out loudest at the first tutti, the opposite of the other two. In the middle, where the instrument groups take the theme in turn, it drops one notch.
Unlike the other two, it plays loud from the very first sound and keeps the gap between quiet and loud narrow. Its loud passages also last the longest.
At 2:36 it is the longest of the three. The first sound is also the softest, and it stretches the quiet passage out the longest before rising at the end.

headline_en: Another climax 30 seconds from the end
note_en: About 30 seconds before the end it rises once more, as loud as the climax. Just before that it drops to its smallest, then swells in one move.
Later than the other two, it reaches its loudest at the very end. Before that it swells loudly once, pulls back, and builds up again.
The first sound is the quietest of the three. In the big passage it reaches near-maximum twice and sustains it longer than the other two.
Earlier than the other two, it reaches near-maximum within 30 seconds. After the climax it reaches near-maximum two more times.
At 3:02 it runs about 10 seconds longer than the other two. It sinks the middle lowest of the three and keeps its loud passages the shortest.
Unlike the other two, it rises once ahead of time around the middle. The big passage is built up in several stages until it reaches the top.
Alone among the three, it reaches its loudest in the middle. After that it sinks deep, and its loud passages are the shortest.
It doesn't drop low at the start or in the middle. It draws things out evenly, begins to grow, and reaches the climax within 10 seconds.
At 8:03 it is about 30 seconds shorter than the other two. It touches the top briefly, then comes back down to very quiet within 16 seconds.

headline_en: A cry held back to the end
note_en: It saves the loudest sound until about 10 seconds before the end. It sustains loud playing the longest of the three.

headline_en: Bursts out loud, then quickly small
note_en: It flings out the first gesture loudly, then drops to its quietest within 14 seconds. The gap between quiet and loud is bigger than in the Arditti and Italiano quartets.
It sets the ending down quieter than either of the other two. Its loud passages are also the shortest, and the gap between quiet and loud is the widest.
It opens louder than the other two. The climax arrives about 15 seconds later.
Unlike Dohnányi, it opens quietly. The ending is less quiet, and it carries loud playing the longest.
At 2:38 it runs more than 20 seconds longer than the other two. It doesn't make the whisper as small as the Arditti and Emerson quartets do, and it reaches near-maximum early.
In the big passage at the start it already rises to near-maximum. It lowers the middle the least of the three.

headline_en: Maximum only seconds from the end
note_en: It doesn't get near maximum until a few seconds before the end. Unlike Yuja Wang, it carries the middle very quietly.

headline_en: Maximum at both front and back
note_en: It opens at near-maximum from the start. It sustains loud playing longer than the other two and rises to that level once more late on.
It keeps a quiet level steady and rises loud exactly once. Apart from that one moment there is almost no loud playing.
The first sound is the loudest of the three, and the levels before and after stay the most even. There is no deep drop anywhere.
It starts far quieter than the other two. From there it grows little by little.

headline_en: Keeps its force in the middle too
note_en: At 2:35 it runs 22 seconds longer than Rozhdestvensky. Even in the middle tune it eases the level down only slightly, and in the later part it blasts out at maximum twice.

headline_en: First maximum only after the tune
note_en: At 2:13 it is the shortest of the three. It sinks the middle tune the deepest, and only after that reaches maximum for the first time.
It reaches near-maximum within 11 seconds. It carries loud playing longer than the other two.
After the first tutti it sinks deep, then builds up again and rises to its loudest. After that it continues one notch lower.

headline_en: The first tutti is the climax
note_en: Alone among the three, it places the loudest sound at the first tutti. The gap between quiet and loud is also narrower than in the other two.
After playing its loudest, it sets the ending down much lower than the other two. The time it spends at loud levels is also the shortest.

headline_en: Deep after the climax, then loud again
note_en: After the first tutti it comes down only one notch, then rises to its loudest. After that it cuts back the deepest of the three and swells once more.

headline_en: Maximum from the first big passage
note_en: At 4:07 it runs 15 seconds longer than Järvi. From the first big passage it plays near-maximum and sustains loud playing the longest of the three.
Alone among the three, it plays its loudest at the final chord. It comes down deep once before the end, then builds all the way to the finish.
At 3:06 it is the shortest of the three. It comes in loud from the start, barely changes level, and holds loud playing the longest.

headline_en: Trumpet version, built up from soft
note_en: It starts quieter than the other two and builds toward the end. The gap between quiet and loud is large, and it pushes on loudly right to the finish.
At 6:35 it is more than twice as long as Yo-Yo Ma's performance. It opens quietly, reaches near-maximum in under two minutes, then carries the middle section loudly for a long stretch.
The cello opens quietly and, together with the orchestra, rises to its loudest right in the middle. It swells loudly once more later and ends softly.

headline_en: A surge in the final stretch
note_en: It starts the quietest and opens the widest gap between quiet and loud of the three. The final third surges far louder than the front.
At 7:07 it runs about two and a half minutes longer than the guitar version. It comes in loud from the start and holds loud playing the longest.
At 4:41 it is shorter than the other two. The front, middle and back carry on at similar levels, and the loud playing is brief.
It reaches near-maximum earlier than the other two. It pulls back a long way in the middle, then rises to the same level again late on.
At 4:47 it runs about a minute longer than the other two. Its loud playing is the shortest of the three, and it is the last to reach near-maximum.
At 4:51 it runs about 45 seconds longer than the other two. It doesn't reach near-maximum until the final 40 seconds.

headline_en: One big swell at the end of the first verse
note_en: At the end of the first verse it swells loudly once, takes a breath, and builds again. It closes the quietest of the three.
The first sound is quieter than in the other two. It builds step by step, and the ending is, if anything, less soft.
It reaches its loudest the latest of the three, near the end. Before that it also rises to near-maximum twice.

headline_en: Shortest, held back then released at once
note_en: At 4:38 it is nearly four minutes shorter than the two-piano version. It holds back near-maximum until past the midpoint, then rises all at once.
At 8:37 it is longer than the other two. It starts the quietest and reaches its loudest about a quarter of the way in.
At 7:00 it is the longest of the three. The melody passes from instrument to instrument, rising loud again and again.
It runs a minute and a half longer than the voice version. Drawing out a single long note, it rises to its loudest in the middle.
At 4:58 it is the shortest of the three. It rises and falls within a quiet range, and grows loudest only near the end.
It rises loud in five places, all at similar levels. It doesn't hold back the ending as much as Gruberová does, and raises it a little further at the last.

headline_en: Pushed up in the last 30 seconds
note_en: It runs 6 seconds shorter than Bernstein and 17 seconds shorter than Myung-Whun Chung. It keeps the middle low and reserved, then climbs to its loudest over the final 30 seconds.
At 2:01 it is the longest of the three. It lets the level fall between phrases less than the other two do, and builds the volume step by step.

headline_en: Maximum right after the quiet passage
note_en: As soon as the quiet passage in the middle ends, it reaches near-maximum. It rises to that level several more times afterward, and unlike the other two it doesn't save the ending.

headline_en: Maximum held back to the end
note_en: It never reaches near-maximum until 16 seconds before the end. The quiet passage in the middle is also the deepest of the three, and it swells loudly just once at the close.
It pulls back sharply in the middle, then builds for nearly 30 seconds to reach the climax. Unlike Zimerman, it rises to near-maximum once more 10 seconds later.
It takes over 30 seconds on the eight bars of bell-like chords, more than 10 seconds longer than the other two. As soon as the theme enters, it reaches near-maximum.

headline_en: Swells and settles with each phrase
note_en: Unlike Myung-Whun Chung, it swells every phrase loudly and then settles deeply. Before the final climax it pulls back the deepest, then climbs in two stages.

headline_en: Still loud in the last 20 seconds
note_en: From the first chord it starts the least quietly of the three. In the last 20 seconds too, it keeps up a loud level and doesn't come down as far as the other two.
At 1:48 it runs about 10 seconds shorter than the other two. It builds the hymn gradually from the start, and doesn't sink the quiet passage as deep as the other two do.

headline_en: Two fortissimos at an even level
note_en: It strikes the first fortissimo and the second theme at almost the same level. The woodwind passage between them is sunk deeper than Solti does.
It sinks the quiet passage the deepest of the three, so the gap to the loud passages is also the widest. It draws out the hymn 10 seconds slower than Perahia.
Unlike the other two, it blasts loudest at the first fortissimo and drops the second theme one notch. It opens at near-maximum from the very start.

headline_en: Held back until the second theme
note_en: It holds back the opening and the first fortissimo the most of the three. Its loudest sound comes at the second theme.
It sings the first 50 seconds of the hymn at a steady, similar level. Unlike Perahia, it doesn't grow bit by bit, and rises to near-maximum only when it reaches the loud passage.

headline_en: Restrained at first, a long finish
note_en: At 2:40 it is the longest of the three. It holds things quiet for more than the first minute, then sustains the last big passage at near-maximum for nearly 6 seconds.
At 2:06 it is 34 seconds shorter than Fabbricini. It keeps the first rise before the last big passage one notch lower, so near-maximum happens only once.
At 2:20 it falls between the other two performances. Unlike Cotrubaș, it rises to almost the same level before the last big passage too, so there are two big outbursts.
At 47 seconds it is the shortest of the three. At each big passage it climbs back to near the level of the first sound, so the flow is almost the same as Solti's.

headline_en: The opening level to the end
note_en: Unlike Haitink, it keeps the level of the first sound all the way to the end. In the last big passage before the finish, it rises as loud as at the start.

headline_en: A step below after the first sound
note_en: Only the first sound is at maximum; alone among the three, it sings the later big passages one step below that. At 51 seconds it is 4 seconds longer than Rattle.
It lowers the passage that turns quiet again after the first tutti less than the other two do. The loudest sound comes in the exposition, and the ending is almost as loud.

headline_en: The fastest Aria of the three
note_en: At 3:41 it is 21 seconds shorter than Hewitt and 14 seconds shorter than Perahia. The repeat is played as loudly as the first time, and the climax comes in the repeat of the second half.

headline_en: A narrow gap between cry and prayer
note_en: Even when the women's voices enter, it lowers the level far less than Davis does. It goes in at near-maximum from the first outcry, and swells loud earlier than Karajan.
It opens the quietest of the three and lowers the passage leading into the recapitulation just as much. The loudest sound comes at the final chord.
Unlike the other two, it holds back the first outcry a little and plays the second outcry the loudest. The closing prayer passage runs more evenly than in the other two.
At 2:43 it runs about 20 seconds longer than the other two. Each time the women's voices enter, it sinks the deepest of the three, setting up a strong contrast with the outcries.
Unlike Schiff, it lowers the level every time it plays the same half again. The second half is raised loud the first time, but on the repeat it is played as small as the first half.

headline_en: Near maximum from the first tutti
note_en: It already bursts out at near-maximum at the first tutti. It doesn't lower the quiet passage as far as Karajan does, and the loudest sound comes at the final chord.
From the first sound it opens less quietly than the other two, and it already reaches near-maximum in the first half. On the repeat it lowers the level like Hewitt, but not as much.
It plays in the same order as Tharaud and runs 19 seconds longer. After sinking deep once in the middle, it carries the second half at near-maximum and ends loudly.
At 1:08 it is the shortest of the three. After about 10 seconds it drops one notch, then rises to near-maximum within 18 seconds.

headline_en: Near maximum only in the last 20 seconds
note_en: Unlike Yo-Yo Ma, it never reaches near-maximum until 20 seconds before the end. In the final climb it rises all at once.
At 2:22 it is the longest of the three. It plays the middle one step lower for over 30 seconds, then rises loud near the end.

Alone among the three, it plays the first refrain one more time, which makes it about 8 seconds longer. Right after its loudest moment it drops sharply, and unlike the other two it doesn't rise loud again to the end.
At 2:36 it is the longest of the three. It opens very quietly, and sinks deeper than the other two once more in the early part.
About two-thirds of the way through, it sinks the deepest and longest of the three. Going into the ending it doesn't pull back as far as the other two.
At 1:44 it is 38 seconds shorter than Gould. It reaches near-maximum within 15 seconds and doesn't change the level much until just before the final chord.
It pushes at near-maximum for longer in the later passage past the two-thirds mark than in the big passage in the middle. The other two put more weight on the middle.
It reaches near-maximum in one minute and carries the whole second half loudly. The quiet passages near the end aren't sunk as deep as in the other two.
Unlike the other two, it opens very quietly. It builds step by step for over a minute, pulls back once before the climax, then rises.
At 3:24 it runs more than 30 seconds longer than the other two. With 30 seconds to go it falls very quiet for nearly 10 seconds, then rises loud again.

headline_en: One step higher at each climax
note_en: It sets the first climax the lowest of the three and raises each following climax by one step. Once it enters the big passage, it doesn't come down for over 40 seconds.
The flow is almost the same as Harnoncourt's. The final orchestral passage continues at the same level as the start, and unlike Harnoncourt it doesn't sink.
At 3:04 it is 33 seconds shorter than the other two. It builds the quiet introduction bit by bit and rises to its loudest within 30 seconds.
The way it raises the level with each choral line is almost the same as Herreweghe's. But it sinks the final orchestral passage far lower than at the start before closing.
It lowers the quiet passage in the middle less, and sinks the one that turns quiet again right after it deeper. It also opens the first orchestral passage quietly, setting it against the chorus.
After the first chord it rises to near-maximum again in the second big passage. The quiet passage after that is shorter than in Kanneh-Mason's.

headline_en: Loud only in the two middle lines
note_en: It is the shortest of the three. Even when the chorus enters it is mostly quiet, rising loud only in the two middle lines and dropping deep again straight away.
Right after the quiet passage in the middle, it already rises to near-maximum. The other two hold that level back for about another minute.
It sinks the quiet passage in the middle the deepest of the three, then rises loud immediately. It saves near-maximum until 70 seconds before the end.
The quiet passage in the middle of the introduction is the deepest of the three. The big passage that rises again later isn't raised as high as in Yo-Yo Ma's and Schiff's.
The first 40 seconds before it rises loud are longer and quieter than in the other two. Right before the first climax it pulls back deep, then climbs loud within 7 seconds.
Like Kremer, it draws out the introduction for nearly 40 seconds, but grows a little all the while. In the middle of the later quiet passage it rises loud once and then comes back down.

headline_en: A softer end to the introduction
note_en: It draws out the introduction for over 40 seconds, dropping softer just before it begins to swell. Unlike Perlman, it never raises the later quiet passage loud for nearly a minute.
It stays loud for over 18 seconds from the first chord, about 8 seconds longer than the other two. It passes through the quiet passage in the middle much more shallowly than Kanneh-Mason does.
Unlike Domingo, it sings the first climax almost as loud as the last. The second climax is at almost the same level as the first.

headline_en: A step back after the first chord
note_en: At 1:36 it runs over 5 seconds longer than the other two. After the first chord of the brass theme it steps back, then rises loud again in the repeat.
At 3:55 it runs over 24 seconds longer than the other two. In the fast passage it pulls back deeply several times and then surges again.
At 1:18 it is 15 seconds shorter than Boulez and 37 seconds shorter than Karajan. After the very loud spot it never climbs again, and descends steadily to the end.
It holds the quiet passage in the middle at the lowest level of the three throughout. It opens the fanfare quieter than the other two, too, and builds up loudly.
It plays the fugato for solo piano the quietest of the three. At the big climax it hits near-maximum briefly three times.

headline_en: Quiet passages not lowered as much
note_en: It lowers the D minor passage and the closing passage less than the other two. It also rises to the big climax earlier than the other two and keeps it loud for over 40 seconds.
After one loud hit on the very strong chord, it rises louder about 10 seconds later. Its time at near-maximum is the shortest of the three.
It sustains the loud passage about 10 seconds longer than the other two. Unlike Solti, it doesn't come down deep at the end and closes loudly.
It lowers the D minor passage deeper than the other two. At the big climax it holds near-maximum as one block for over 20 seconds.
It drives the whole last minute close to near-maximum. It lowers the quiet passage in the middle less than Muti does.
It reaches near-maximum the moment it enters the fast passage. Except for one break, it never backs off, and it sustains loud playing the longest of the three.

headline_en: Maximum held back to the end
note_en: Throughout the fast passage it pushes along one step lower, reaching near-maximum only about 40 seconds before the end. The other two get there within the first 40 seconds.

headline_en: Maximum only at the final chord
note_en: It opens the fanfare loudly from the start and saves near-maximum for the very last chord. The other two reach it once earlier, after two minutes.
At 1:55 it runs over 20 seconds longer than the other two. After the climax it sustains loud playing for over 30 seconds, and rises once more about 30 seconds before the end.
It opens the strings the loudest of the three, so the gap to the brass theme is small. Toward the end, unlike Dudamel, it comes down deep.

headline_en: The loudest sound in the final section
note_en: It plays the opening theme far lower than the final section, and the A major section in the middle slightly higher than that. It also sinks the quiet passages the deepest of the three.

headline_en: The most unhurried of the three
note_en: At 3:55 it is the longest of the three. It opens louder than the other two from the start, and brings the big early passage close to the level of the last.
It already plays its loudest in the strong passage of the early theme. It pushes the final section just as hard, and unlike Zimerman it doesn't save it for the end.
At 1:24 it falls between the other two performances. Around 20 seconds it moves up one step and walks at the same level for over 30 seconds, then rises again at the loud chord.
At 3:29 it is 26 seconds shorter than Yeol Eum Son. It keeps the early big passage low and raises everything at once in the last big passage.

headline_en: Loud from the first strong passage
note_en: At 4:11 it is the shortest of the three. It plays near-maximum from the first strong passage, and sinks the quiet passage after the climax very deep.

headline_en: Loud even in the quiet march
note_en: At 1:13 it is the shortest of the three. It rises close to maximum right in the middle of the quiet march, so the gap to the loud-chord passage is small.
It plays the early strong passage louder than Zimerman, and carries the final section loudly for about 30 seconds longer than Zimerman.
After the climax it lowers the quiet passage as deep as Shelley does, then rises loud once more at the A major close. Shelley doesn't build the close that much.
The loudest sound, which Ashkenazy places at the start and Pollini toward the back, this one places right in the middle. It drops low once early on, then grows toward the middle.

headline_en: Near maximum in the first 4 seconds
note_en: It reaches near-maximum within the first 4 seconds and puts its loudest sound at the beginning too. The other two play their loudest after more than a minute.
At 4:50 it runs 39 seconds longer than Shelley. It doesn't lower the quiet passages as deep as the other two, and carries the loud passage at the climax longer.

headline_en: Quiet up to the loud chords
note_en: At 1:31 it runs 18 seconds longer than Argerich. It holds a quiet walk low for over a minute, then rises all at once at the loud chords.

headline_en: A final section with no retreat
note_en: It pushes the last big passage loudly for nearly a minute without once backing off. The other two come down once before it, then rise again.
The difference in level is the smallest of the three, so it pushes evenly from start to finish. Its loudest sound comes about 20 seconds before the end.
It reaches, just short of four minutes in, the level that the other two hit at the orchestral opening. The early step back is also the deepest of the three.

headline_en: Low until a minute before the climax
note_en: It sets the early climb the lowest of the three and rises all at once from a minute before the climax. Soon after the climax it rises loud once more.
facts_en: Academy of St Martin in the Fields

headline_en: The deepest end of the oboe passage
note_en: Even when the theme repeats it pushes near-maximum. The very quiet spot at the end of the oboe passage is sunk the deepest of the three.
It plays near-maximum only once, in the first third. Its length is similar to Böhm's, but it lowers the middle less than Böhm does.
facts_en: Academy of St Martin in the Fields

headline_en: A step lower after the climax
note_en: It builds the climb in the middle loudly too, and plays the climax in one go. Unlike the other two, it doesn't rise loud again after the climax and continues one step lower.
Unlike the other two, it already lowers the level when the theme repeats. At 1:01 it is 9 seconds shorter than Böhm.
facts_en: Academy of St Martin in the Fields

note_en: At 7:04 it runs about 55 seconds longer than the other two. It rises to its loudest where the orchestra rounds off the theme, and unlike Pires it doesn't hold back until the second half.
facts_en: Marriner · Academy of St Martin in the Fields

note_en: At 4:57 it is over 40 seconds shorter than the other two. It climbs close to near-maximum far more often than Böhm does.
It holds the middle the lowest of the three and has only two brief loud spots. At 5:50 it runs 53 seconds longer than Harnoncourt.
At 8:33 it runs over a minute longer than the other two. It holds loud for 40 seconds around the climax, drawing it out over 15 seconds longer than the other two.
At 1:10 it runs 9 seconds longer than Marriner. The flow is almost the same as Bernstein's, but it lowers the oboe passage less than Bernstein does.

headline_en: Maximum at the first wind chord
note_en: It already reaches its loudest at the opening chord, where the winds cut in strongly. Unlike Pires, it reaches near-maximum several more times early on.
It is 34 seconds shorter than Bernstein and 18 seconds shorter than Nézet-Séguin. In the big passage at the end, it spends the least time at near-maximum of the three.

headline_en: One big swell in the middle
note_en: Like Gardiner, it comes in loud from the start, but it rises once more right in the middle and then returns to the earlier level.
It is 1:22 shorter than Fischer-Dieskau. It rises loud in several places, and closes the final minute a step quieter than the other two.

headline_en: Opens soft, building to the middle
note_en: It opens quieter than Gardiner and Daucé, and grows bit by bit toward the middle. It touches near-maximum only briefly and soon eases back.
It plays its loudest around the 30-second mark. It doesn't sink the middle as deep as Yunchan Lim does, and eases down gradually over the last 30 seconds.
There are fewer places where the level drops far during the singing than in the other two. It opens less quietly, right from the string prelude.
facts_en: Paavo Järvi · Estonian National Symphony Orchestra

note_en: It has more places where it rises loud than the other two. The loudest sound comes about a minute before the end.
It doesn't sink far in the middle either, and spaces its loud rises evenly in several places. The loudest sound comes right in the middle.
At 3:55 it runs 34 seconds longer than Myung-Whun Chung. It doesn't rise loud until the big passage near the end, but once there it never comes down from near-maximum.
Unlike Leonhardt, it doesn't open quietly; it rises loud within 30 seconds and keeps that level to the end. It plays loud for the longest time of the three.
It raises the middle peak louder than the other two. In the big passage at the end it reaches near-maximum, steps back once, then rises again.
At 2:24 it is the shortest of the three. In the middle it sinks far quieter than the other two, then afterward rises to its loudest.
It is similar in length to Goerne's, but rises high in only one place. The rest continues evenly at similar levels.
It runs around a minute longer than the other two. It opens the prelude the quietest of the three, and its quiet passages are more frequent and deeper than in the other two.

headline_en: An aria over a minute longer
note_en: At 8:07 it runs over a minute longer than the other two. It rises loud in several places, but reaches near-maximum only once.
It gathers its loudest sound at the peak in the middle and carries it loudly for nearly 10 seconds. Unlike Perlman, it keeps the early part one step lower.
The other two rise in one go with 30 seconds left, whereas Bernstein climbs in two stages starting earlier. Just before the last climb that performance pulls back once.
At each passage of resolve it rises loud briefly and then comes right back down. It spends a third as long at loud levels as Bartoli does.
facts_en: Marriner · Academy of St Martin in the Fields

headline_en: Near maximum only at the end
note_en: It unfolds 10 seconds slower than Lupu and 6 seconds slower than Pollini. It builds up gradually, reaching near-maximum only in the last few seconds.
After the orchestral introduction it carries the piano theme at the most even level of the three. It rises loud again in the last phrase to close.
The opening, where the midnight bell tolls, is the loudest of the three. It rises in one go with 30 seconds left, and the last 14 seconds run at near-maximum to the end.

headline_en: A step down at the end
note_en: It enters quieter than the other two and builds gradually. Unlike the other two, after the climax it finishes a step lower.
It plays 30 seconds slower than Hilary Hahn and 34 seconds slower than Perlman. The opening and the quiet passage after the climax are the quietest of the three.
It is 5 seconds longer than Argerich. Like Lang Lang, it builds the last phrase again, but sinks deeper before it.
The other two are loudest around the middle, but Perlman's version already reaches maximum at the one-third mark. It doesn't sink the quiet passages deep either, keeping an even course.
It holds a quiet level until just before the climb, then rises in one go, more steeply than Stokowski. It steps back once and then carries on loudly to the end.
It is 10 seconds faster than Ashkenazy. It climbs to near-maximum the earliest of the three, takes one breath, then rises to maximum again at the end.
Right after its loudest cry, it drops deep. The gap between quiet and loud is the widest of the three.
At 2:35 it runs over 20 seconds longer than the other two. In the last 45 seconds it climbs close to near-maximum four times, more than the other two.

headline_en: Loud in the middle, soft at the end
note_en: It rises close to near-maximum in the middle of the piano theme. Unlike the other two, it doesn't build the last phrase and closes it softly.
The two orchestral tuttis and the final chord ring out at almost the same level. The quiet passages aren't as deep as in the other two either, so the range of levels is small.
It rises to its loudest less than a minute after the alto enters. The later phrase continues almost as loud, and unlike Bernstein it doesn't hold back to the end.
It is 17 seconds shorter than Konwitschny and 31 seconds shorter than Haitink. It holds back the first surge a step and rises to its loudest in the second surge.

headline_en: One in the middle, maximum at the end
note_en: It rises loud once in the middle phrase, and saves the loudest sound for near the end. It rises loud later than Boulez and earlier than Bernstein.
It rings out loudest at the first tutti, and the second tutti is one step lower. The final chord closes as loud as the first tutti.
It already rises loudest in the first surge, and the second is played at almost the same level. Unlike the other two, it doesn't hold back the first surge.

headline_en: An ending louder than the first chord
note_en: At 6:31 it is 1:30 shorter than Karajan. The Statue's first chord also rings loud, but the loudest sound is saved for the end, when Giovanni is dragged down to hell.
facts_en: Academy of St Martin in the Fields

note_en: The quiet passage between the two surges is the deepest of the three. It holds back the first surge for a long time, and puts its loudest sound in the second.

headline_en: Maximum at the Statue's first chord
note_en: It rings the Statue's entrance chord the loudest. After that it presses the dialogue passage the lowest of the three, then raises it again at the end.

headline_en: A final chord louder than the tuttis
note_en: Both tuttis are quieter than the final chord, so the loudest sound comes at the end. The quiet passages are also the deepest of the three.

headline_en: Maximum only in the last 10 seconds
note_en: It doesn't rise loud for the first time until 10 seconds before the end. For over two minutes before that it runs the quietest of the three.
It runs over 1:20 longer than the other two. Even in the dialogue in the middle it rises to near-maximum several times, and carries almost the whole last minute loudly.
The first 7 seconds are very quiet, and then it starts to grow. It is 21 seconds shorter than Bernstein and 7 seconds shorter than Abbado.
It sets the first f the lowest of the three and grows loudly up to ff. The loudest sound comes at the second peak.
At the end, where the music turns to D minor and the orchestra comes in strongly, it holds loud the longest of the three. It keeps that level through the spot where Bernstein soon lets go.
It carries the latter part of the prayer melody close to maximum longer than the other two. The loudness of the trumpet call falls between Bernstein's and Levine's.
All three trumpet calls are close to the loudest sound of the prayer melody. In the last descent of the prayer melody it quiets earlier than the other two.
It is 16 seconds shorter than Karajan and 21 seconds shorter than Chailly. It reaches the peak where the horn soars after 50 seconds, touches maximum briefly, then drops a step.
It is 21 seconds longer than Karajan and 14 seconds longer than Abbado. Unlike the other two, it swells loudly once 14 seconds after the start.
The opening isn't as quiet as in the other two, so even when the horn enters it doesn't swell suddenly but rises steadily. Its length falls between Thielemann's and Chailly's.
It is near maximum from the start, and its loudest sound comes at the first ff. The second peak is a step lower but runs on later than in the other two.

headline_en: Both peaks at the same level
note_en: It plays the first ff peak and the second peak at almost the same level. The span of its swell from the first f to ff falls between Abbado's and Solti's.
It holds the peak where the horn soars near maximum the longest of the three, reaching maximum twice. When it builds up again at the end, it rises close to that peak as well.
It is 15 seconds longer than Mehta and 12 seconds longer than Bernstein. The trumpet call sits a step lower, and the loudest sound comes in the latter part of the prayer melody.
The gap between quiet and loud is smaller than in the other two. It opens the first tutti a step lower and rises to near-maximum from the middle on.

headline_en: A hushed end to the introduction
note_en: After the introduction's crescendo it stays very quiet for over 20 seconds. That quiet passage is the longest of the three, and the introduction's length falls between Perlman's and Mutter's.
The orchestra rings out loudly from the first call, so the climb to ff is the narrowest of the three. The piano theme also continues evenly without large swings.
The introduction takes 1:28, 15 seconds shorter than Kremer's and 27 seconds shorter than Perlman's. The first chord is also quieter than in the other two.
At 7:56 it is 27 seconds shorter than Perahia. It reaches near-maximum at each loud passage, and its quiet passages aren't deep, so the range of levels is small.
At 2:50 it is 29 seconds shorter than Thunemann. From the first tutti to the last, it rings out the loud places at almost the same level.

headline_en: A slow pace of over nine minutes
note_en: At 9:04 it is 58 seconds longer than Kissin. It sets the first unison a step lower, and rings out the recapitulation's unison and the final chord at near-maximum.
It builds the orchestral crescendo to a range between the Zimerman version and the Rubinstein version. In the middle of the piano theme it pulls back deep once, then rises again.

headline_en: Maximum in the last few bars
note_en: It doesn't reach near-maximum for the first time until a few seconds before the end. The gap between quiet and loud is also narrower than in the other two.
At 8:06 it is the shortest of the three. It rings out near-maximum from the first unison, and the quiet passages aren't as deep as in the other two.
At 3:19 it is the longest of the three. It extends the final tutti beyond 30 seconds, and its quiet passages are deeper than in the other two.

headline_en: A crescendo built from the floor
note_en: It starts the orchestral crescendo far lower than the other two. It brings out the piano theme softly and grows toward the end, and it is about 3 seconds shorter than the other two.

headline_en: Maximum held back until 30 seconds from the end
note_en: It never reaches near-maximum until about 30 seconds before the end. All the loud passages before that finish one step lower.
The introduction takes 1:55, 27 seconds longer than Mutter's. Its biggest peak is much bigger than in the other two, close to the level of the Presto.
At 8:23 it is the longest of the three, and its quiet passages are deeper than in the other two. Both of the big passages late in the exposition ring out at near-maximum.
It rises to near-maximum at every loud passage and sinks the spaces between them the deepest of the three. Its swings are far bigger than Tjeknavorian's.
facts_en: Performance used in "2001: A Space Odyssey"

headline_en: Maximum only at the last peak
note_en: It plays near-maximum only at the final climax. The quiet passage in the middle is also far less deep than Nott's.
At 4:22 it is over 40 seconds shorter than the other two. It is loud from the first sound, and the loud level stays even until 20 seconds before the end.
It rises to near-maximum within 45 seconds. Unlike Lesne, it reaches that level many times all the way to the end.
At 4:13 it is about 37 seconds shorter than the other two. It reaches near-maximum only twice in the latter part, and carries the rest one step lower.
The opening is the quietest of the three, and so is the gap between quiet and loud. Near-maximum appears only twice.
At 47 seconds it is 4 to 5 seconds shorter than the other two. It brings out the cello theme very quietly, but doesn't lower the second quiet passage as much as Karajan does.
It sinks the quiet passage in the middle the deepest of the three. After that it rises to near-maximum twice.
It lowers the cello theme after the two chords, and the second quiet passage after that, equally deep. Harnoncourt doesn't lower the second as much.
The cello theme after the two chords is the least quiet of the three. At 52 seconds it is 5 seconds longer than Harnoncourt.
It first reaches near-maximum a minute later than Mead. In the later part it repeatedly rises loud and sinks deep.

headline_en: Maximum again a minute from the end
note_en: After rising to its loudest within the first minute, it continues the middle one step lower, unlike the other two. A minute before the end it rises to near-maximum again.

headline_en: Near maximum from the first peak
note_en: It already rises to near-maximum at the first big peak. The last climax arrives over 20 seconds later than Gielen's.
Its quiet passages are the deepest and longest of the three. It reaches near-maximum only once, 1:20 before the end.

headline_en: Near maximum four times late on
note_en: In the second half it reaches near-maximum four times. Though its length is almost the same as Kermes's, it plays loud far more often.

headline_en: A climax in the first part
note_en: At 9:42 it is longer than the other two. Already near the end of the first part it sings as loud as in the middle section, and it empties out the later quiet passage deeply.
The gap between quiet and loud is the smallest of the three. It reaches near-maximum from the first part, and its later quiet passage isn't as deep as in the other two.
The quiet passage in the middle isn't as deep as in the other two. It reaches near-maximum in the final variations and pushes loudly to the end.
As soon as the racing passage starts, it reaches near-maximum and pushes at that level until it ends. Unlike Dutoit, it doesn't build up within it.

headline_en: The first part a step below
note_en: It places the first part a step below the other two, and reaches near-maximum only in the big middle passage. It empties out the later quiet passage as deep as Reuss does.
Late in the piece it sinks deeper than the other two, twice. Then near the end it rises to its loudest to close.

headline_en: Near maximum from the first theme
note_en: The near-maximum level that the other two reach only in the final variations, it reaches already in the first theme. Just before the final variations it is quiet for over 25 seconds.
At 6:08 it is the shortest of the three. It sinks the quiet variations in the middle far deeper than the other two, then rises in one go in the final variations.
At 4:13 it is over 20 seconds longer than Fleming. After the big passage early on, it draws out the quiet passage longer and deeper than the other two.
At 3:50 it is the shortest of the three. It reaches near-maximum within a minute and doesn't press the quiet passages as deep as the other two.

headline_en: Built up in the last seconds
note_en: At 3:00 it is the longest of the three. It carries the racing passage one step lower at an even level for over 10 seconds, then rises to its loudest only in the last few seconds.
The introduction is quieter than in the other two. In the racing passage it rises close to near-maximum within a few seconds and continues evenly.
Each time it restarts quietly after a crescendo, it drops the deepest of the three. It holds the final diminished-seventh chord for over 6 seconds before slowly letting go.

headline_en: Maximum already at the first peak
note_en: It is about 8 seconds shorter than the other two. It already plays its loudest at the first peak, and releases the final diminished-seventh chord after about 4 seconds.

headline_en: Straight on up after the second
note_en: It places the second motif a step lower than Böhm does, and then, without sinking as much as the other two, keeps building up to the final chord.
At 1:38 it is the shortest of the three. It already rises close to near-maximum at the second motif and holds that level for the 20 seconds before the final chord.

headline_en: Maximum only at the final chord
note_en: At 1:57 it is 19 seconds longer than Böhm. It leaves the quiet passages between the motifs longer than the other two do, and reaches maximum only near the final chord.

headline_en: Maximum saved for the final chord
note_en: It sets the two earlier peaks a step lower, and plays loudest only at the final diminished-seventh chord. It holds that chord as long as Horowitz does.
